pos: n. (proper name; a ford or place on the Jordan)
etymology: Hebrew Beth-barah, apparently house of the ford or place of crossing, from beth (house, place) with an element connected to passing over.
biblical_def: Bethbarah is named twice, both in one verse: “And Gideon sent messengers throughout all mount Ephraim, saying, Come down against the Midianites, and take before them the waters unto Bethbarah and Jordan. Then all the men of Ephraim gathered themselves together, and took the waters unto Bethbarah and Jordan” (Judges 7:24). The battle was already won. Three hundred men with trumpets, pitchers and lamps had stood still around the Midianite camp while the LORD set every man's sword against his fellow, and the host had broken and run east for the river. Gideon's order to Ephraim is the closing of a trap: hold the fords, so the fleeing army cannot cross. Bethbarah is where the crossing was stopped. The dictionary marks two things. First, that God won the victory with three hundred so that Israel could not say her own hand had saved her — and then used the whole of mount Ephraim to finish it, for He is not sparing of His people's labour once He has secured their humility. Second, that a rout must be pressed to the water. A defeated enemy allowed to cross the river returns, and Gideon knew it.

corruption_summary: Gideon's three hundred are read as a tactical anecdote; the text gives the reduction a stated doctrinal reason.
corruption_paragraphs: The story of the three hundred is endlessly retold as a lesson in small-unit boldness. Judges 7:2 forecloses that reading by stating the purpose outright: the people were too many for God, lest Israel should say her own hand had saved her. The reduction from thirty-two thousand to three hundred was not a tactical choice; it was the removal of every ground for boasting.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God arranges His victories so that the glory cannot be misassigned. He then called Ephraim to the fords, which is the other half of the lesson: humbled men are not idle men. The LORD who will not share the credit does not withhold the work.

pos: n. (proper name; a place on the border of Judah and Benjamin)
etymology: Hebrew Beth-choglah, commonly read house of the partridge, from beth (house, place) and a word for that bird. The Authorized Version spells it Bethhoglah at Joshua 15:6 and 18:19, 21.
biblical_def: Bethhogla is named in the surveying of the land: “And the border went up to Bethhogla, and passed along by the north of Betharabah; and the border went up to the stone of Bohan the son of Reuben” (Joshua 15:6). It sat near the north end of the Dead Sea, in the hot trench of the Jordan, and it served as a marker where Judah's northern line and Benjamin's southern line met; Joshua 18:19 traces the same point from Benjamin's side and assigns the town to Benjamin. These border chapters are the least-read pages in Joshua and among the most important. They are the title deeds. God had sworn the land to Abraham, and here the oath is reduced to surveyed lines, named landmarks, and a stone with a man's name on it. A promise that can be walked, measured and disputed over is a promise that has landed in the world. “There failed not ought of any good thing which the LORD had spoken unto the house of Israel; all came to pass” (Joshua 21:45). The partridge-house on the salt flats is one of the survey pegs by which that sentence can be checked.

corruption_summary: Boundary lists are dismissed as tedious filler; they are the recorded discharge of a sworn promise.
corruption_paragraphs: The allotment chapters of Joshua are skipped by most readers and are commonly treated by critics as an idealised map drawn long after any such division occurred. The dictionary holds them as survey record. Their texture argues for it: the lines run from a named spring to a named ridge to a stone that belonged to a particular man, which is how real boundaries are described and not how ideals are drawn.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God's promises terminate in facts. The land sworn to Abraham in a vision was delivered as acreage with corners, and Joshua 21:45 dares the reader to audit it. A faith whose promises never touch the ground is not the faith of this book.

pos: n. (proper name; a son of Eshton in the genealogy of Judah)
etymology: Hebrew Beth-rapha, house of Rapha or house of the healer, from beth (house) with the element rapha. The form is a place-name used as a personal name, or a clan named as a man.
biblical_def: Bethrapha is named once: “And Eshton begat Bethrapha, and Paseah, and Tehinnah the father of Irnahash. These are the men of Rechah” (1 Chronicles 4:12). The verse sits in the long Judah genealogy of 1 Chronicles 4, and its names have the shape of places as often as of persons — house of Rapha, father of Irnahash (city of Nahash), the men of Rechah. Hebrew genealogy moves between a man and the settlement his family became without marking the transition, because to the Hebrew mind they were not separable: a house was both the people and the place. The dictionary records this plainly rather than forcing a choice the text does not make. What the passage shows is the density of God's record of the tribe of promise. Judah is given four chapters while whole tribes get a dozen verses, and the reason surfaces at the end of the book: it was from Judah that the King would come. The genealogy is thick where the promise runs, and a name like Bethrapha is written down because it stood in the line that mattered most.

corruption_summary: Names that hover between person and place are called confusion; in Hebrew a house is both the family and its ground.
corruption_paragraphs: Genealogies in which a name may denote a man or a town are routinely treated as evidence of garbled sources. The ambiguity is in the Hebrew conception, not in the record. A beth is a household and the household's place at once, and a founder's name passing to his settlement is the ordinary course of things, not a copyist's error.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the purposeful weighting of Scripture's records. Judah receives four chapters of genealogy because the sceptre was promised to Judah, and the Chronicler is building toward the house of David. “For it is evident that our Lord sprang out of Juda” (Hebrews 7:14). The crowded lists are the paper trail of the incarnation.

pos: n. (proper name; a town of Gad in the valley east of Jordan)
etymology: Hebrew Beth-haram, house of the height, from beth (house) and a word for height or elevation. Numbers 32:36 gives the related form Bethharan among the cities Gad built.
biblical_def: Betharam is named once, in Gad's allotment: “And in the valley, Betharam, and Bethnimrah, and Succoth, and Zaphon, the rest of the kingdom of Sihon king of Heshbon, Jordan and his border, even unto the edge of the sea of Chinnereth on the other side Jordan eastward” (Joshua 13:27). The phrase that carries the weight is the rest of the kingdom of Sihon king of Heshbon. Sihon had refused Israel passage and come out to fight at Jahaz, and his kingdom was taken; and the land of a king who would not let Israel pass became the inheritance of two and a half tribes. Betharam stands in the valley portion of that spoil. The dictionary notes the pattern, because it recurs: Pharaoh hardened himself and Israel went out with the wealth of Egypt; Sihon refused the road and lost the country; Haman built a gallows and hanged on it. God is not obstructed by opposition; He is served by it. “Surely the wrath of man shall praise thee” (Psalm 76:10). A town in the Jordan valley bears witness to a king who said no to the people of God and whose whole realm became their farmland.

corruption_summary: The conquest of Sihon is read as aggression; Scripture records a refused passage answered by a judgment long foretold.
corruption_paragraphs: Israel's taking of the Transjordan is commonly described as simple expansionism. The narrative is more specific. Israel asked leave to pass along the highway and promised not to turn into field or vineyard; Sihon refused and attacked; and the land fell. Numbers volunteers the request and the refusal, which an account constructing a pretext would have no reason to do.

The principle to recover is that opposition to God's purpose becomes its instrument. Sihon's refusal did not delay Israel by a season; it enlarged her by a kingdom. “Surely the wrath of man shall praise thee” (Psalm 76:10), and the towns of the valley, Betharam among them, were the proof of it to every Gadite who farmed there.

pos: n. (proper name; a mountain or place at the northern limit of Israel's territory)
etymology: Hebrew Ba'al-chermon, lord of Hermon or Baal of Hermon — the name of the Canaanite god attached to the great northern mountain, a witness in the place-name itself to the worship that had been practised there.
biblical_def: Baalhermon is named twice, each time as a boundary of the far north: “the Hivites that dwelt in mount Lebanon, from mount Baalhermon unto the entering in of Hamath” (Judges 3:3), and “they increased from Bashan unto Baalhermon and Senir, and unto mount Hermon” (1 Chronicles 5:23). Hermon is the snow-capped mass at Israel's northern end, and the mountain had been a seat of Baal worship; the compound name preserves that history. Judges 3 names it in a passage of great importance, for it explains why these nations were left in the land at all: “they were to prove Israel by them, to know whether they would hearken unto the commandments of the LORD” (Judges 3:4). The Canaanites who remained were a test, deliberately left. The dictionary marks the severity and the mercy of that arrangement. God does not always remove the occasion of sin from His people; He often leaves it in place, within sight, to show them what is in their hearts. Half the tribe of Manasseh grew prosperous up to the slopes of a mountain named for a demon, and in time they went after the gods of the land.

corruption_summary: Temptation left in place is read as divine negligence; Judges states that the nations remained in order to prove Israel.
corruption_paragraphs: That God left Canaanite nations in the land is often treated either as a failure of the conquest or as evidence of a disunited text. Judges 3:4 gives the reason in a single clause: they were to prove Israel, to know whether she would hearken. The remaining nations were not an oversight; they were an examination, and the book of Judges is the record of Israel sitting it repeatedly and failing.

The principle to recover is that trial is a divine method, not a divine lapse. “And thou shalt remember all the way which the LORD thy God led thee these forty years in the wilderness, to humble thee, and to prove thee, to know what was in thine heart” (Deuteronomy 8:2). A Christian who expects every occasion of sin to be removed from his path has mistaken the nature of sanctification; God commonly leaves the mountain standing and teaches us to walk past it.

pos: n. (proper name; the place of Solomon's vineyard in the Song)
etymology: Hebrew Ba'al-hamon, commonly read lord of a multitude or place of abundance, from ba'al (lord, owner) and a word for a crowd or great quantity.
biblical_def: Baalhamon is named once, and in a telling place: “Solomon had a vineyard at Baalhamon; he let out the vineyard unto keepers; every one for the fruit thereof was to bring a thousand pieces of silver” (Song of Solomon 8:11). The verse opens the Song's closing comparison. Solomon's vineyard at the place of abundance was a commercial holding farmed by tenants for a fixed rent of a thousand pieces of silver — and the bride answers it in the next breath: “My vineyard, which is mine, is before me: thou, O Solomon, must have a thousand, and those that keep the fruit thereof two hundred” (Song of Solomon 8:12). Her vineyard is her own, held and kept and not let out. The contrast is the Song's last word on love: a thousand-silver estate worked by hirelings set against one vineyard its owner tends herself. This is the same book that says “love is strong as death” (Song of Solomon 8:6), and it ends by refusing to let love be let out at rent. The dictionary reads the Song as what it is — a true song of marriage between one man and one woman, and therefore a figure of Christ and His church.

corruption_summary: The Song is read as either mere eroticism or mere allegory; it is a true marriage song and therefore a figure of Christ and the church.
corruption_paragraphs: Two opposite errors attend this book. One empties it of its plain subject and makes it allegory only, embarrassed by the body. The other empties it of covenant and makes it an anthology of desire, indifferent to whether the lovers are married. The dictionary holds the historic Reformed reading: the Song celebrates the love of one husband and one wife, and precisely because that love is covenantal it figures Christ and His church (Ephesians 5:31-32).

The principle to recover is that love is not a commodity. Solomon's vineyard at Baalhamon was leased for silver; the bride's vineyard is her own and before her. “If a man would give all the substance of his house for love, it would utterly be contemned” (Song of Solomon 8:7). A culture that treats intimacy as a market is answered by the last paragraph of this book, where the rented estate is named only to be set beside something that cannot be rented.

pos: n. (proper name; the idol Israel served at Shechem after Gideon's death)
etymology: Hebrew Ba'al-berith, lord of the covenant, from ba'al (lord) and berith (covenant) — the same word used of the LORD's covenant with Israel, here attached to an idol.
biblical_def: Baalberith is named twice: “And it came to pass, as soon as Gideon was dead, that the children of Israel turned again, and went a whoring after Baalim, and made Baalberith their god” (Judges 8:33); and then the money: “And they gave him threescore and ten pieces of silver out of the house of Baalberith, wherewith Abimelech hired vain and light persons, which followed him” (Judges 9:4). The name is the horror of the thing. Berith is the covenant word — the word of Sinai, of Abraham, of David — and Israel took it and hung it on an idol, making a lord of the covenant who was not the LORD who made the covenant. And the temple treasury of this counterfeit financed Abimelech's murder of seventy of his brothers on one stone. That is the arithmetic of the chapter: seventy pieces of silver from the house of the false covenant-lord bought the deaths of seventy sons of the man who had delivered Israel. Counterfeit religion is never merely mistaken; it funds atrocity. The verse immediately before says the cause: “And the children of Israel remembered not the LORD their God, who had delivered them” (Judges 8:34).

corruption_summary: Counterfeit religion borrows the true faith's vocabulary; Baalberith wore the covenant word while funding murder.
corruption_paragraphs: The most dangerous false religion is not the one that denies the words of the true but the one that keeps them. Israel did not abandon the language of covenant; she transferred it to an idol and called him lord of the covenant. Every later counterfeit works the same way, retaining grace, covenant, gospel, and love while emptying each of its content, which is why the dictionary insists on naming frameworks by their actual names rather than accepting their self-descriptions.

The principle to recover is that borrowed vocabulary is no evidence of a true faith, and that doctrinal corruption bears practical fruit. The treasury of Baalberith paid for the slaughter of Gideon's seventy sons. A religion that keeps the covenant word and loses the covenant God will not stay harmless, and Judges 9 is the chapter that shows what it buys.

pos: n. (proper name; a city of Hadadezer from which David took brass)
etymology: Hebrew Berothai, commonly connected with a word for cypresses or for wells. The Chronicler's parallel names the city Chun, and the margin at 1 Chronicles 18:8 notes the correspondence.
biblical_def: Berothai is named once: “And from Betah, and from Berothai, cities of Hadadezer, king David took exceeding much brass” (2 Samuel 8:8). The Chronicler gives the same campaign with different city-names and adds what became of the metal: “Likewise from Tibhath, and from Chun, cities of Hadarezer, brought David very much brass, wherewith Solomon made the brasen sea, and the pillars, and the vessels of brass” (1 Chronicles 18:8). Follow that sentence. Brass taken from a Syrian king's cities became the great laver in which the priests washed, and the two pillars Jachin and Boaz that stood at the porch of the temple. The spoil of a war became the furniture of worship, because David dedicated it: “Which also king David did dedicate unto the LORD, with the silver and gold that he had dedicated of all nations which he subdued” (2 Samuel 8:11). He did not build the house; he gathered the material and gave it away to a son who would. The dictionary marks the pattern: a man may spend his life assembling what another will use, and the brass of Berothai stood in Solomon's temple because David would not keep it.

corruption_summary: Labour whose fruit another man enjoys is counted loss; David gathered a temple he was forbidden to build.
corruption_paragraphs: The age measures a work by whether the worker sees it finished and gets the credit. David spent decades and a fortune gathering gold, silver, brass, timber and stone for a house the LORD told him plainly he would not build, and he handed the whole of it to Solomon with instructions. He is nowhere recorded as resenting it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God divides a work among generations and no part of it is wasted. The brass of Berothai was carried off by a soldier and shaped by his son into the sea where priests washed. “One soweth, and another reapeth” (John 4:37) is not a complaint in Scripture; it is how the kingdom is built.

pos: n. (proper name; a town of Judah that received a share of David's spoil)
etymology: Hebrew Kor-'ashan, apparently furnace of smoke or smoking furnace, from a word for a kiln or furnace with an element meaning smoke. It is generally identified with the Ashan of Joshua 15:42.
biblical_def: Chorashan is named once, in a list of towns that received a present: “And to them which were in Hormah, and to them which were in Chorashan, and to them which were in Athach” (1 Samuel 30:30). The setting is one of the finest things David ever did. The Amalekites had burned Ziklag and carried off the wives and children of David's whole company, and the men had spoken of stoning him; he encouraged himself in the LORD his God, pursued, and recovered all. Then, instead of keeping the spoil, he sent portions throughout the towns of southern Judah where he and his men had ranged during the years of running from Saul: “Behold a present for you of the spoil of the enemies of the LORD” (1 Samuel 30:26). Chorashan got a share. And note what he had already settled on the way home, when the men who had stayed with the baggage were to be cut out: “as his part is that goeth down to the battle, so shall his part be that tarrieth by the stuff” (1 Samuel 30:24). A fugitive with nothing, newly plundered, established a rule of equity and then gave the surplus away.

corruption_summary: Generosity is thought to require surplus; David gave away spoil recovered on the day his own house had been burned.
corruption_paragraphs: It is assumed that giving waits on security — that a man shares once his own position is safe. 1 Samuel 30 inverts it. On the day David's city was ash and his own family had just been recovered, with his men lately talking of stoning him, he fixed an equal share for those too faint to fight and then distributed presents across a dozen towns of Judah.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that faith gives out of a God-ward security rather than a material one. David encouraged himself in the LORD his God before he did any of it, and the order matters: strength in God first, equity second, generosity third. Chorashan received a gift from a man who had been homeless that morning.

pos: n. (proper name; the place where Judah's third son Shelah was born)
etymology: Hebrew Kezib, from a root meaning to lie or to deceive — hence falsehood or deceitful, a name often given to a stream that fails in summer. It is generally identified with the Achzib of Joshua 15:44.
biblical_def: Chezib is named once: “And she yet again conceived, and bare a son; and called his name Shelah: and he was at Chezib, when she bare him” (Genesis 38:5). The chapter is the sordid interlude in the Joseph narrative, and the place-name is almost too apt, for Chezib means deceit, and deceit is the whole subject of Genesis 38. Judah married a Canaanite; his two elder sons died under God's hand; he withheld Shelah, the son born at Chezib, from Tamar his widowed daughter-in-law, promising and not performing; and Tamar answered deception with deception, veiled herself by the road and conceived by Judah himself. Judah's own verdict closes it: “She hath been more righteous than I; because that I gave her not to Shelah my son” (Genesis 38:26). Out of that squalid business came Pharez, and from Pharez the line ran to David and to Christ: “And Judas begat Phares and Zara of Thamar” (Matthew 1:3), where Matthew names Tamar in the genealogy of the Lord rather than quietly omitting her. Grace is not embarrassed by the house it comes through.

corruption_summary: Genesis 38 is read as an embarrassment to be explained away; Matthew puts Tamar in the Lord's genealogy on purpose.
corruption_paragraphs: Genesis 38 is handled either as a misplaced fragment interrupting the Joseph story or as a passage best not read aloud. Both miss its function. It is set exactly where it is to show what the house of Judah was while Joseph was being made a saviour in Egypt, and its product is Pharez, through whom the sceptre promised in Genesis 49:10 descends.

The principle to recover is that grace runs through a line it does not excuse. Scripture tells the truth about Judah — a Canaanite marriage, a broken promise to a widow, a roadside transaction with a woman he took for a harlot — and then Matthew names Tamar among the Lord's forebears. The genealogy of Christ is not a monument to the respectability of his ancestors; it is a record of mercy reaching a family born at a place called Deceit.
